questions.q: Which HTTP method is idempotent by contract?
options: POST, because servers deduplicate repeated form submissions automatically
PATCH, because partial updates always converge to one final state
PUT, because replaying the same full replacement yields the same state
CONNECT, because tunnels are established at most one time per client

questions.q: A request lacks valid credentials vs a valid user lacking permission. Which codes apply?
options: 400 for missing credentials, 401 for missing permission
401 for missing or invalid credentials, 403 for insufficient permission
403 for missing credentials, 404 to hide protected resources
401 for both cases, distinguished only by the response body

questions.q: In REST semantics, what should GET requests never do?
options: Return different representations based on Accept headers
Include query parameters that filter the returned collection
Return large paginated collections without compression enabled
Cause observable state changes on the server beyond logs or caching

questions.q: What is the main reason to version a public API (e.g., /v2/)?
options: To ship breaking changes while existing clients keep working
To let the server cache each client's responses separately
To meet HTTP requirements that URLs must encode a version
To reduce payload sizes by silently dropping deprecated fields

questions.q: What is offset pagination's basic mechanism?
options: The server streams the whole collection and clients discard the extras
Clients pass how many rows to skip and how many rows to return
The server remembers each client's position in a session store
Clients pass the ID of the last seen row to anchor the next page

questions.q: Which is a defining trait of gRPC compared with typical REST/JSON?
options: gRPC responses are human-readable text, easing debugging in browsers
gRPC requires no schema, while REST mandates an OpenAPI contract
gRPC runs only over UDP for lower latency than TCP-based REST
gRPC uses binary protobuf over HTTP/2 with generated client stubs

questions.q: Why should DELETE be idempotent?
options: Retries after timeouts must converge to the same end state safely
Servers are required to return 200 on every repeated delete attempt
Clients are technically unable to send the same request twice
Proxies automatically replay DELETE requests to improve reliability

questions.q: What is the purpose of a machine-readable error body (e.g., problem+json)?
options: It lets proxies rewrite error responses into redirects automatically
It replaces HTTP status codes, which clients are meant to ignore
Clients can branch on stable error codes instead of parsing prose
It hides stack traces by encrypting diagnostic details for support staff

questions.q: A user pages through offset-paginated results while rows are being inserted. What symptom appears?
options: The database locks the table until the client finishes paging
Rows shift between pages, so items repeat or get skipped
Offsets beyond 1000 return errors on most SQL databases
Responses interleave rows from other users' concurrent sessions

questions.q: Why do cursor (keyset) APIs typically not support jumping straight to page N?
options: Cursors encode a position, not an ordinal; reaching page N means walking pages in order
Cursors expire after one use, so page numbers cannot be revisited later
Serving page N would require the server to hold a long-lived read transaction open per client
Keyset queries only support descending sort orders on primary keys

questions.q: A client retries POST /payments after a timeout. How does an Idempotency-Key header help?
options: It instructs the gateway to convert the POST into a safe PUT request
It makes the server reject all duplicate submissions with 400 errors permanently
The server stores the first result per key and replays it for retries
It forces the client to wait for a webhook instead of a response

questions.q: When is gRPC a poor fit versus REST/JSON?
options: Internal microservice calls that need low latency and typed contracts
Streaming telemetry between backend services in one data center
Polyglot service meshes where teams want generated client stubs
Public browser-facing APIs where plain HTTP and JSON tooling matter

questions.q: Which of these changes to a stable API is a breaking change?
options: Adding a new optional field to an existing response object
Adding a new endpoint under the same version prefix
Documenting an existing but previously undocumented header
Renaming an existing response field consumed by clients

questions.q: What is the semantic difference between PUT and PATCH?
options: PUT replaces the full resource; PATCH applies a partial modification
PUT creates only; PATCH is the only method allowed to update
PATCH is idempotent by contract while PUT is explicitly not
PUT is for JSON bodies while PATCH is reserved for form encoding

questions.q: An API returns 200 with an error field in the body on failures. Why is this harmful?
options: Because the HTTP specification strictly forbids returning response bodies for failed requests
Monitoring, caches, and retry logic keyed on status codes misread failures as successes
Clients cannot parse JSON bodies once a request has actually failed
Load balancers drop 200 responses that contain error fields in the body

questions.q: What should a well-designed 429 rate-limit response include?
options: A permanent ban notice so abusive clients stop retrying forever
An alternate mirror URL that clients can hit while throttled
A Retry-After hint and stable error code so clients back off correctly
A reduced-quality response body instead of an outright rejection

questions.q: A bulk update of 500 items partially succeeds. What is the best response design?
options: Per-item results with stable codes (207-style) so clients retry only failures
Return 200 whenever any item succeeded, listing the failed IDs inside a response header
Return 400 for the whole batch whenever any single item fails
Process asynchronously and always return 202 with no status endpoint

questions.q: A REST API fronts a long-running video transcode. What is the standard pattern?
options: Hold the original HTTP connection open until the transcode finishes, however many minutes that takes
Return 200 immediately and let clients guess when the output is ready
Require clients to open a WebSocket for every submitted transcode job
Return 202 with an operation URL clients poll (or a webhook) for completion

questions.q: URL versioning vs header versioning: what is the honest tradeoff?
options: Header versioning breaks HTTP caching entirely and is therefore never used in practice
URL versioning lets a single client freely mix API versions per request, while header versioning cannot
URL versions are explicit and cache-friendly but multiply endpoints; header versions keep URLs stable yet are easy to miss
URL versioning requires a separate DNS zone per version, which header versioning avoids

questions.q: Mobile clients on flaky networks call six endpoints to render one screen. What is the best remedy?
options: Raise per-endpoint rate limits so all six calls can complete faster
Provide an aggregated endpoint (or BFF) returning the screen's data in one round trip
Migrate all six endpoints to gRPC bidirectional streaming so they can share one TLS session
Cache each endpoint's response in localStorage for later offline reuse
